name: Uriah
bio:
Uriah the Hittite was a soldier in David's army, husband of Bathsheba, whose quiet integrity stands in stark contrast to David's conduct through this whole episode. While Uriah was away at the siege of Rabbah, David saw his wife Bathsheba from the palace roof and took her; when she conceived, David recalled Uriah from the battlefield under the pretense of asking about the war, hoping he would go home to his wife and the child could be passed off as his own (2 Samuel 11:1-8). But Uriah slept at the entrance of the palace with the king's guards instead, and when David asked why, he answered, "The ark and Israel and Judah are staying in tents, and my commander Joab and my lord's men are camped in the open fields. How could I go to my house to eat and drink and sleep with my wife? As surely as you live, I will not do such a thing!" (2 Samuel 11:9-11). David tried again the next night, getting Uriah drunk, but Uriah still would not go home (2 Samuel 11:12-13).

With every attempt at concealment failed, David sent Uriah back to the battle carrying his own death warrant: a sealed letter to Joab ordering that Uriah be placed in the fiercest fighting and then abandoned, so that he would be struck down. Joab carried out the order, positioning Uriah where the defenders of the city were strongest; Uriah died there along with other soldiers, and Joab sent word to David carefully instructing the messenger how to soften the report of these losses if David grew angry (2 Samuel 11:14-24). When Bathsheba heard her husband was dead, she mourned for him; after the mourning period, David brought her into his house as his wife. Uriah's death, Scripture states plainly, was the thing that "displeased the LORD" and set in motion Nathan's rebuke and its lasting consequences for David's household (2 Samuel 11:25-27; 12:9-10).
